food.text: Buddhist influence discouraged meat eating in Japan, yet mentions of eating wild boar and deer persisted from the 8th century into the 16th century. These animals were not covered by Emperor Tenmu's ban. Game meat was centered in the mountains of northern Japan, but it was also sold in markets in more urban areas.
food.source_title: History of meat consumption in Japan

food.text: Records from the Middle Ages may give some idea of the dishes people enjoyed in Japan, but they do not give the details needed for accurate recipes. Anything like a recipe from the Middle Ages is a rare commodity in Japan or in any country.

Korean mandu, a filled dumpling, is said to have arrived in Korea through the Mongols in the 14th century. Its name is cognate with Chinese mantou and Japanese manjū, though the modern Chinese and Japanese counterparts mostly refer to different dishes.

As the new bushi warrior class rose, mammals were increasingly hunted in Japan. Descriptions of the warriors' lives mention them feasting on deer, wild boars, bears, raccoon dogs (tanuki), serows, rabbits, and otters.
food.source_title: History of meat consumption in Japan

food.text: Trade with Siam (Thailand) brought Thai indica rice to the Ryukyu Kingdom. From the 15th century it was used to distill awamori, an Okinawan spirit.

In the 13th century, some shrines, including Suwa Shrine in Shinano Province and Utsunomiya Shrine in Shimotsuke Province, accepted offerings of meat, particularly deer or other hunted animals. Suwa Shrine adopted and created Buddhist doctrine that legitimized such sacrifices as "compassionate killing" that helped the salvation of the killed animals' souls.
food.source_title: History of meat consumption in Japan

food.text: Pigs were first introduced to the Ryukyu Kingdom by Chinese immigrants in 1392. They failed to become a widespread part of Ryukyu diet and culture because there was not enough food to feed the pigs themselves.
food.source_title: History of meat consumption in Japan

art.text: Dating from about 1130, the Genji Monogatari Emaki is the earliest surviving yamato-e handscroll and one of the high points of Japanese painting. It illustrates The Tale of Genji, a novel written about the year 1000 by Murasaki Shikibu. Its 12th-century artists devised pictorial conventions to convey the emotional content of each scene.

Korean celadon pottery was the most famous art produced by Goryeo artisans, made from circa 1050 CE to 1250 CE. Although celadon originated in China, Korean potters created their own unique style of pottery.
Painting in the Goryeo period (918 to 1392) was dominated by Buddhist scroll paintings that adapted Chinese styles. About 160 of them survive from the period.

Until the late 15th century, both religious and secular arts flourished in Japan. After the Ōnin War (1467 to 1477), the country entered a period of political, social and economic turmoil that lasted for over a century.

During the Muromachi period, Korean influence on Japanese painting reached its peak. Korean art and artists frequently arrived on Japan's shores, shaping both the style and theme of Japanese ink painting. Historian Sokuro Wakimoto called the years 1394 to 1486 the "Era of Korean Style" in Japanese ink painting.

The priest-painter Shūbun was a monk at the Kyoto temple of Shōkoku-ji. His painting Reading in a Bamboo Grove (1446) is a realistic landscape with deep recession into space, and he is counted among the foremost artists of the Muromachi period.

Unlike most artists of his period, the priest-painter Sesshū was able to journey to China and study Chinese painting at its source. His Landscape of the Four Seasons (c. 1486) is one of his most accomplished works, showing a continuing landscape through the four seasons.
The Goryeo court founded a royal artist's school or academy, the Dohwaseo. It held examinations for artists and was run by bureaucrats of the court.

The two most important Japanese ink painters of the Muromachi period were Shūbun and Sumon. Shūbun's art displays many characteristic features of Korean painting, and Sumon was himself an immigrant from Korea.

In the second half of the 12th century, a livelier style of continuous narrative illustration became popular in Japan. The Ban Dainagon Ekotoba, a scroll about an intrigue at court, shows figures in active motion, painted in rapid brush strokes and thin but vibrant colors.

Jinsa, or underglaze red, is a technique that uses copper oxide pigment to create copper-red designs. It was developed in Korea during the 12th century and later inspired the underglaze red ceramics of the Yuan dynasty.

King Gongmin of Goryeo (1330 to 1374) was a significant painter of his period. Outside the Buddhist tradition, the court painter Yi Nyeong and the scholar-painter Yi Chehyŏn are also considered significant Goryeo artists.

Yi Su-mun, considered the founder of the Soga school of Japan, returned from Korea to Japan in 1424 as a boat-companion of the older priest-painter Shubun of Shokokuji. He was known in Japan as Ri Shubun. He painted alongside and influenced the originals of Japanese zen art.

war.text: Between 1231 and 1259 the Mongols campaigned against Goryeo, with six major campaigns in 1231, 1232, 1235, 1238, 1247 and 1253. Parts of Gyeongsang and Jeolla were ravaged. Between 1253 and 1258, Möngke Khan's general Jalairtai Qorchi launched four devastating invasions against Korea at tremendous cost to civilian lives throughout the Korean Peninsula. The repeated invasions brought havoc, loss of human lives and famine, and in 1232 the Mongols destroyed the Tripitaka Koreana woodblocks.
The Kamakura shogunate repelled Mongol invasions of Japan in 1274 and 1281. It was eventually overthrown by Emperor Go-Daigo.

As the Mongol army and Hong Dagu withdrew to their ships, the Japanese army conducted night attacks and killed as many soldiers as they could. On the night of October 19, a typhoon caused one-third of the returning ships to sink, and many Mongol soldiers drowned. The typhoon was called the Kamikaze, meaning "divinely conjured wind".

The Genpei War (1180–1185) was fought between the Taira and Minamoto families. It ended at the naval Battle of Dan-no-ura in 1185, where Minamoto no Yoshitsune won a decisive victory. Yoritomo and his retainers thus became the de facto rulers of Japan.

The Ōnin War began in 1467 and devastated much of Kyoto. It accelerated the decline of the Ashikaga shogunate, whose shōguns kept their office but had ever less control over the provinces. Conventionally, it marks the start of the Sengoku period.

From 1033 to 1044 Goryeo built a stone wall in the northern Korean peninsula, roughly 1000 li long and about 24 feet high and wide. King Deokjong ordered Yuso to build the defenses in response to incursions by the Khitan of the northwest and the Jurchen of the northeast. It ran from the mouth of the Yalu River to around Hamheung.

In early October 1274, the Battle of Bun'ei began when a combined force of Mongols and Koreans arrived by ship. They seized Tsushima, Iki island and other islands. The Mongols slaughtered the inhabitants of Tsushima, and about 1000 Japanese soldiers were killed on Iki island.

In 1156, a dispute over succession to the throne erupted, and the two rival claimants, Emperor Go-Shirakawa and Emperor Sutoku, hired the Taira and Minamoto clans in the hope of securing the throne by military force. In the war that followed, the Taira clan led by Taira no Kiyomori defeated the Minamoto clan. Kiyomori used his victory to accumulate power for himself in Kyoto and even installed his own grandson Antoku as emperor. The outcome set the Minamoto and Taira against each other, and their power struggle led to the Heiji rebellion in 1160.

In 1460, shōgun Ashikaga Yoshimasa abdicated in favor of his younger brother Ashikaga Yoshimi, and Yoshimasa's wife Hino Tomiko strongly opposed this. She won the support of Yamana Sōzen and other samurai leaders and went to war against Yoshimasa's supporters, especially the Hosokawa clan. This dispute started the Ōnin War.
At the Battle of Torikai-Gata, the samurai Takezaki Suenaga and Shiraishi Michiyasu killed 3,500 Mongols. It was the second Japanese victory after the Mongols landed on Kyushu.

In 1180, Taira no Kiyomori was challenged by an uprising led by Minamoto no Yoritomo, a member of the Minamoto clan whom Kiyomori had exiled to Kamakura. Kiyomori died in 1181, but the ensuing bloody Genpei War (1180–1185) between the Taira and Minamoto families continued for another four years. It ended in 1185, when a force commanded by Yoritomo's younger brother, Minamoto no Yoshitsune, scored a decisive victory at the naval Battle of Dan-no-ura.

Tomoe Gozen was a servant of Minamoto no Yoshinaka and one of the famous female warriors, or onna-musha, of the Genpei War. She helped Yoshinaka defend himself against his cousin Minamoto no Yoritomo's forces, especially at the Battle of Awazu in 1184.
In 1485, the Yamashiro ikki expelled two competing Hatakeyama armies from southern Yamashiro. It then administered the area through an association of local warriors and communities until 1493.
When the Mongols reached Kyushu, they met the first real Japanese army. At the Battle of Akasaka, the forces of Kikuchi Takefusa won with a surprise attack.

literature.text: Kyoto ceased to be the sole literary centre of Japan in the medieval period. Important writers and readerships appeared throughout the country, and new forms developed, such as renga linked verse, otogi-zōshi prose narratives and the theatrical form noh.

In medieval Japan, Kyoto ceased to be the only literary centre. Important writers and readers appeared throughout the country, and new forms developed such as the gunki monogatari and otogi-zōshi prose narratives, renga linked verse, and theatrical forms such as noh.

During the Kamakura period (1185–1333), Japan went through many civil wars, which led to the rise of a warrior class and to war tales, histories and related stories. The Tale of the Heike is an epic account of the struggle between the Minamoto and Taira clans for control of Japan at the end of the 12th century. Work from this period is notable for a more somber tone than earlier eras, with themes of life and death, simple lifestyles, and redemption through killing.

The Samguk sagi (1146) and Samguk yusa (1285) were two great historical records compiled in Classical Chinese during the Koryo era. They preserved the myths, legends and folktales of the Three Kingdoms and Silla, and remain the basic sources for such material.

The Samguk yusa was compiled by a Zen master, so it includes the lives of Buddhist saints, the origins of monasteries, stupas and bells, and accounts of miracles performed by Buddhas and bodhisattvas. Its tales are rich in shamanist and Buddhist elements, and it also includes 14 hyangga.

Yongbi och'on ka, or Songs of Flying Dragons, was compiled between 1445 and 1447. It is the most representative akchang, a poetic form that flourished briefly in the 15th century, and it is a cycle in praise of the founding of the Yi dynasty.

During the Muromachi period, cultural activity spread through all levels of society and classical court literature gradually disappeared. New genres such as renga linked verse and Noh theater developed among the common people, while Buddhist priests created setsuwa such as the Nihon Ryoiki for preaching.

In 1383, the warrior leader Shiba Yoshimasa completed the Chikubashō, a one-volume set of precepts for the young men of the Shiba clan. Its title translates as The Bamboo Stilt Anthology, and it combined the ethical morality of the warrior with the tasteful lifestyle of the aristocracy.

Korean poetry was originally meant to be sung, and its forms reflect its melodic origins. Its prosody is based on a line of alternating groups of three or four syllables, which is probably the most natural rhythm to the language.

Growing public interest in travel and pilgrimages, along with the development of roads, made travel literature more popular. Notable travel diaries include Fuji kikō (1432) and Tsukushi michi no ki (1480).

Imagawa Ryōshun, a general who had taken Buddhist vows, was admired for balancing the military and literary arts. His letter of regulations to his brother Tadaki was used by warrior bureaucrats before the Ōnin War of 1467, and remained popular until World War II.

The Tale of the Heike was composed in the early 13th century to commemorate the stories of courageous and devoted samurai. Among them was Tomoe Gozen, servant of Minamoto no Yoshinaka, who helped defend him against his cousin Minamoto no Yoritomo, especially at the Battle of Awazu in 1184.

In 1256, Hōjō Shigetoki, the Shogunal Deputy in Kyoto, wrote a letter to his son and the house elders of his clan. Now known as The Message of Master Gokurakuji, it emphasized the importance of loyalty to one's master.

science.text: In 1234, during the Goryeo period, Ch'oe Yun-ŭi invented metal movable type printing. The invention made printing easier and more efficient, and it also increased literacy.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Korea

science.text: The Hwacha, first built in 1377 in Goryeo, is widely considered the first true multiple rocket launcher. One of its key features was that it could fire up to 200 rockets at one time, a vast improvement over earlier rocket weapons.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Korea

science.text: In 1402, Korea produced the Kangnido, a map of the world. It was made by combining Chinese, Korean and Japanese maps.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Korea

science.text: Ch'oe Mu-sŏn, a medieval Korean inventor, military commander and scientist, brought widespread use of gunpowder to Korea for the first time. Impressed, the Koryo court and King U built him a laboratory and a factory for gunpowder. He invented the first Korean cannons and the Singijeon fire arrows.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Korea

science.text: During the late Goryeo Dynasty, Goryeo was at the cutting edge of shipboard artillery. In 1356 early experiments were carried out with gunpowder weapons that shot wood or metal projectiles. In 1373, incendiary arrows and "fire tubes", possibly an early form of the Hwacha, were placed on Korean warships.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Korea

science.text: The Kangnido world map was created by Kim Sa-hyeong, Yi Mu and Yi Hoe. It was made in the second year of the reign of Taejong of Joseon.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Korea

science.text: Chinese visitors to Goryeo observed that literacy was so important there that it was considered shameful not to be able to read. This came in a period when Ch'oe Yun-ŭi's metal movable type had made printing easier and increased literacy.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Korea

science.text: Ch'oe Mu-sŏn learned about gunpowder from a Chinese merchant named Lee Yuan, even though sharing it was against Mongol law. Lee was reluctant at first, but came around because he was impressed by Ch'oe's patriotism and determination. The weapons were needed because Japanese pirates, the Wokou, frequently raided Korea's coasts.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Korea

science.text: The Goryeo practice of placing cannons and other gunpowder weapons on ships continued well into the Joseon period. By 1410, over 160 Joseon warships had cannons on board.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Korea

science.text: The Mongol Empire later adopted Korea's movable type printing, and it spread as far as Central Asia. There is conjecture about whether Ch'oe Yun-ŭi's invention influenced later printing inventions such as Gutenberg's printing press.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Korea

politics.text: In 1180 Minamoto no Yoritomo, whom Taira no Kiyomori had exiled to Kamakura, led an uprising against the Taira. The bloody Genpei War between the Taira and Minamoto families lasted from 1180 to 1185. It was sealed in 1185 when a force commanded by Yoritomo's younger brother Minamoto no Yoshitsune scored a decisive victory at the naval Battle of Dan-no-ura. Yoritomo and his retainers thus became the de facto rulers of Japan.

In 1392, General Yi Sŏng-gye led a successful coup to take political power in Korea from the King. His followers forced him to take the crown as Taejo of Joseon, which established a new dynasty. The kingdom he founded lasted 505 years.

In 1156 a dispute over succession to the throne erupted, and the rival claimants Emperor Go-Shirakawa and Emperor Sutoku hired the Taira and Minamoto clans to secure the throne by military force. The war fed a rivalry between the two clans that led to the Heiji rebellion in 1160.

Joseon joined the Imperial Chinese tributary system in 1401 in return for recognition. The new regime lacked a royal bloodline and wanted a justification for its rule from other countries such as China. Accepting the tributary system was also the only way to establish diplomatic relations and trade with China.

Joseon installed Neo-Confucianism as the new state's ideology and encouraged Confucian ideals and doctrines in Korean society. Buddhism was accordingly discouraged, and Buddhists occasionally faced persecution. In 1393 Korea was retitled and the capital was moved to modern-day Seoul.

In 1460 shōgun Ashikaga Yoshimasa abdicated his position to his younger brother Ashikaga Yoshimi, but Yoshimasa's wife Hino Tomiko was strongly against the decision. The succession dispute started the Ōnin War (1467–1477) and led to the beginning of the Sengoku period.

After the Taira clan led by Taira no Kiyomori defeated the Minamoto in the war over the 1156 succession, Kiyomori used his victory to accumulate power for himself in Kyoto. He even installed his own grandson Antoku as emperor. Kiyomori died in 1181, but the ensuing bloody Genpei War between the Taira and Minamoto families continued for another four years.

After Goryeo sent tribute in 1020, Liao accepted, resuming nominal tributary relations. The 1022 peace terms were only a "declaration of vassalage" and the release of a detained Liao envoy. Historian Hans Bielenstein argues that this meant the two states made peace as equal partners, and that Hyeonjong kept his reign title.

In 1426, Sejong the Great enacted a law granting government nobi women 100 days of maternity leave after childbirth. In 1430 it was lengthened by one month before childbirth. In 1434 Sejong also granted their husbands 30 days of paternity leave.

philosophy.text: Throughout the Japanese middle ages, many different schools of Buddhism flourished, including Tendai, Shingon, Pure Land, Zen and Nichiren. Over time, Shinto and Buddhism gradually became intertwined in Japanese culture, rather than being viewed as mutually exclusive.

Goryeo, founded in 918 and ruling the Korean Peninsula until 1392, was known, alongside Unified Silla, as the Golden Age of Buddhism in Korea. As the state religion, Buddhism reached its highest level of influence in Korean history, with 70 temples in the capital alone.

In the Korean Joseon dynasty (1392-1897), a resurgent Neo-Confucianism became the dominant school of thought and was promoted by the state. It was led by thinkers such as Zhu Xi (1130-1200), and it also flourished in Song dynasty China.

In the late Heian period (794-1185), pessimism was popular because of a belief that Buddhism would decline during the latter days of this world. The Pure Land movements spread, encouraging anticipation of a "future life" as a way to cope with desperation over "life in this world".
During the Kamakura period (1185-1333), government dominated by the samurai class began. With it, a "new" Buddhism appeared for the newly risen samurai class.

In the eleventh century, the five elements of godai were attributed to esoteric Japanese Buddhism, in relation to gorin, the "five wheels" or "five rings". The elements are earth, water, fire, wind and void.

After the Genpei War, Minamoto no Yoritomo established a military government at Kamakura in 1185. The Zen school of Buddhism was introduced from China in the Kamakura period and became popular among the samurai class.

Godai and gorin also appear in ninjutsu, where they became an essential part of the esoteric ninja teachings called ninpo-mikkyo. Meanwhile, gogyo, which stems from Chinese wuxing, moved into traditional Japanese medicine and exoteric Buddhism.

culture.text: Eisai, a Zen monk who lived from 1141 to 1215, is generally credited with making tea popular in Japan. In 1191 he returned from China with tea-tree seeds, which he planted on the island of Hirado and in the mountains of Kyūshū.

From the end of the 12th century, tea drinking spread to Zen temples, following China's example. The tea was powdered and drunk after being beaten, which is what is called matcha today. In the Middle Ages it became a common drink for the elite.

Eisai gave some of his tea seeds to Myōe, abbot of the Kōzan-ji temple in Kyoto. Myōe planted them in Toganoo and Uji, which became the first major tea plantations in Japan. Toganoo tea was called "real tea" (honcha), while tea grown elsewhere was called "non-tea" (hicha).

Shogun Ashikaga Yoshimasa (1435–1490) built the first tea house that followed the rules of the tea ceremony. This small room in his Higashiyama palace let him display his Chinese objects, called karamono, during tea ceremonies.

The conflict between the northern and southern courts in the Nanbokuchō period and the frequent civil wars of the Muromachi period caused massive social upheaval in Japan. The nobility, already in decline, lost virtually all of their former prestige, and lower classes moved upward to take their place. High-level members of the warrior class took over from the aristocracy as the custodians of culture. Ichiko stresses that this was a period of bloody warfare and tragedy, yet the literature is often lively and bright.
In the 15th century, Uji tea surpassed Toganoo tea in quality. The title of "real tea" then passed to Uji tea. Uji in Kyoto Prefecture still has a long-standing reputation for producing quality teas.

As late as the early eleventh century, Korean bells were still being delivered to many Japanese temples, including Enjō-ji Temple. Many temple bells in Japan were of Korean design and origin. In 1921, eighteen Korean temple bells were designated national treasures of Japan.

Yoshimasa's tea room was styled after the shoin, the study rooms of Zen monks. It had tatami mats on the floor and a study desk built into the wall. These rooms are the ancestors of modern Japanese living rooms.
